groups.title: The paradox of choice
groups.body: Contemporary consumers are confronted with an unprecedented abundance of options, from breakfast cereals to pension schemes. Common sense suggests that more choice must be better, yet some psychologists argue that this proliferation, far from liberating us, can induce paralysis. In one frequently cited experiment, shoppers offered twenty-four varieties of jam were less likely to buy any than those presented with only six. Critics, however, point out that attempts to replicate the finding have produced mixed results, suggesting that the effect may depend heavily on context: when people have clear preferences or genuine expertise, a wider range is welcome rather than burdensome. The lesson may therefore be not that choice is harmful, but that its design matters. Curating options, and helping people to compare them, may do more for satisfaction than simply multiplying them.

groups.title: Green spaces in cities
groups.body: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to look at a claim that is often repeated: that every extra park makes a city measurably healthier. The evidence is, frankly, more nuanced. A large survey of forty cities found that residents living within five minutes' walk of green space reported lower stress. But the effect almost vanished once the researchers accounted for income, which suggests that wealthier districts simply tend to have both parks and healthier residents. That does not mean parks are pointless. Rather, it means planners should avoid treating them as a quick fix, and should pair new green areas with investment in housing and transport.

groups.title: Language and thought
groups.body: The notion that the language we speak shapes the way we think has oscillated between orthodoxy and disrepute for the better part of a century. The strong version, which holds that language determines thought and makes certain ideas literally unthinkable, has long been discredited. What survives is subtler. Speakers of languages that lack words for left and right, relying instead on compass directions, display an uncanny sense of orientation; and the colour terms a language provides appear to affect how swiftly its speakers distinguish between neighbouring shades. Whether such effects reflect merely habits of attention, formed through constant linguistic practice, or a deeper restructuring of cognition remains contested. Sceptics argue that the former interpretation is sufficient and that the latter is an unwarranted leap; proponents counter that the distinction may be less sharp than it appears, since habits of attention, when entrenched, are difficult to tell apart from structures of thought.

groups.title: A panel on remote work
groups.body: Moderator: Professor Hale, many firms are now insisting on a return to the office. Is that justified? Hale: Well, I'd resist the framing. The data do not support the blanket assertion that productivity collapses at home. What they show is considerable heterogeneity: some tasks, particularly those requiring spontaneous collaboration, do suffer, while others improve markedly. So, a one-size-fits-all mandate strikes me as a blunt instrument. Moderator: But surely managers have a point about mentoring junior staff? Hale: They do, and that is the most compelling argument I have heard. Junior employees learn by osmosis, by overhearing and observing, and that is hard to replicate on a video call. Yet the remedy is to target that specific need, not to recall everyone for five days a week.

groups.title: Teenagers and sleep
groups.body: Presenter: Dr Mai, many parents complain that teenagers sleep too late. Is that simply laziness? Dr Mai: Not at all. During adolescence the body clock shifts, so teenagers naturally feel sleepy later in the evening. The problem is that school often starts early, which means many teenagers get around six hours of sleep instead of the recommended eight to ten. Presenter: What are the consequences? Dr Mai: Poor concentration, mood swings, and in some studies, lower exam results.
